words.definition: The bonds and shared values that make people in a society feel connected and willing to cooperate.
words.example: Community centres and public parks play a vital role in fostering social cohesion in diverse neighbourhoods.

words.definition: Treated as unimportant and pushed to the edge of society, with little power or influence.
words.example: Public libraries provide marginalised groups with free access to information and the internet.

words.definition: The unequal distribution of income between the richest and poorest people in a society.
words.example: Widening income inequality can fuel resentment and erode public trust in democratic institutions.

words.definition: A large and often unfair difference between two or more things or groups.
words.example: There remains a stark disparity between the life chances of children born in affluent and disadvantaged areas.

words.definition: Without enough money, education, housing or other things that are necessary for a decent life.
words.example: Children from deprived backgrounds are statistically less likely to go on to university.

words.definition: The ability of people to move to a different, usually higher, social or economic position than their parents.
words.example: Free, high-quality education is widely regarded as the most effective engine of social mobility.

words.definition: A population in which the proportion of older people is increasing.
words.example: An ageing population means that a shrinking workforce must support a growing number of retirees.
collocations: the challenges of an ageing population

words.definition: A system in which the government pays for services such as healthcare, pensions and support for unemployed people.
words.example: Critics claim that an overly generous welfare state can discourage some people from seeking employment.

words.definition: The situation of having no permanent place to live.
words.example: Soaring rents have contributed to a sharp increase in homelessness in major cities.

words.definition: The difference between the average earnings of men and women.
words.example: Several countries now require large firms to publish salary data in an effort to expose and narrow the gender pay gap.

words.definition: An unfair opinion or feeling about a person or group, formed without knowledge or reason.
words.example: Education is one of the most powerful tools for challenging prejudice and the stereotypes that sustain it.

words.definition: To become, or help someone become, fully accepted as part of a group or society.
words.example: Free language classes are essential in helping immigrants integrate into their host society.

words.definition: A way of life or set of values that places great importance on buying and owning goods.
words.example: Some sociologists argue that rampant consumerism has left people materially richer but no happier.

words.definition: Relating to the duties and activities of people as members of their community or town.
words.example: Encouraging young people to volunteer can foster a stronger sense of civic responsibility.

words.definition: Easily harmed physically, emotionally or financially, and therefore in need of protection.
words.example: The state has a duty to protect the most vulnerable members of society, such as the elderly and the disabled.

words.definition: The process by which wealthier people move into a poorer area, improving it but raising prices so that existing residents can no longer afford to live there.
words.example: While gentrification can revitalise run-down neighbourhoods, it often forces long-standing residents out of the area.

words.definition: Wealthy, with a comfortable standard of living.
words.example: In affluent societies, loneliness has arguably become a more pressing problem than material poverty.
